summary: PFF, a sports data company with ~200 employees and ~20 engineers across India, Spain, and the US, faced falling behind competitors. CTO Mike Spitz launched a three-month case study (January–March) pitting two AI-augmented engineers against a ten-person team on the same codebase and customer base. The key reframe shifted from optimizing engineer speed to optimizing agent speed, recognizing engineers are no longer the bottleneck. Results: 25x deployment frequency (2 engineers deploying 5x/day vs 10 engineers once every 5 days), 10x output by blending ticket counts with code complexity, features built in under 2 months vs estimated 4, and customer satisfaction rising from ~7-7.5 to 8.6/10. Scrum did not survive: no standups (tickets auto-update from PR state), no sprint planning (estimates irrelevant when humans aren't the bottleneck), no refinement (happens in spec/LDD flow), and retrospectives replaced by customer satisfaction surveys. The workflow is Spec → agent-generated Lightweight Design Document (informed by prior LDD patterns) → auto-generated non-blocking tickets → PRs, with every-other-day huddles (30–60 min). Code review split: agents handle style/naming, engineers handle system design. A QA agent spins up on staging after each merge, checking acceptance criteria against tickets, with a near-term goal of agents automatically creating fix PRs for failed criteria—enabling parallel self-healing. Humans remain essential for security, product/brand feel, and engineering complexity oversight (LDD prevents over-engineering). Strategic advice: start with boring repetitive tasks engineers hate, remove redundant process, encode engineering culture and patterns (e.g., service repository pattern) in skills, ensure guardrails are functional before autonomous flow, start with the best engineers, avoid onboarding everyone at once, and use a slow phased approach. Small companies have an advantage scaling this; being too conservative risks compounding competitive gaps. Not every engineer thrives—curious, self-directed engineers excel while those needing prescriptive specs struggle.

sections.title: Introduction to PFF and Case Study Context
sections.summary: Spitz introduces PFF as a sports data company serving NFL/NCAA teams with fantasy football and sports betting products. Fully distributed team across India, Spain, and the US with ~200 employees and ~20 engineers. 100M annual page views, 9M annual drafts. Company was falling behind competitors, prompting experimentation with AI tools starting in November before a formal case study from January to March.

sections.title: The Core Reframe: Optimize for Agent Speed
sections.summary: The central question shifted from how to help engineers output more to how to make agents quicker. Historically, engineering perks and Agile practices existed because engineers were the bottleneck. With agents, that bottleneck shifts, enabling fundamentally different organizational optimization.

sections.title: Case Study Results: 25x Deploys, 10x Output, Higher Satisfaction
sections.summary: Two engineers deployed five times daily versus a ten-person team's once every five days (25x). Output was 10x by blending ticket counts with code complexity. Features estimated at four months were built in under two, with one engineer unblocked in under a month. Customer satisfaction rose from ~7-7.5 to 8.6/10 via statistically significant surveys. Caveat: smaller teams are inherently faster, but the small team still had to coordinate with the larger one.

sections.title: Dismantling Scrum and Traditional Processes
sections.summary: Scrum did not survive. No project manager, no standups (tickets auto-update from PR state), no sprint planning (estimates irrelevant when humans aren't the bottleneck), no sprint refinement (happens in spec/LDD flow), no retrospectives (replaced by customer satisfaction surveys and deployment metrics). Engineers flag issues immediately rather than waiting for sprint end.

sections.title: New Development Workflow: Spec → LDD → Ticket → PR
sections.summary: Workflow: agent interviews team to create spec, generates a Lightweight Design Document informed by prior LDD patterns for consistency, distributes for engineer feedback, then auto-generates non-blocking tickets and PRs. Every-other-day huddles (30–60 min) with engineers, product, and design replace ceremonies. MVP deploys to production for rapid feedback.

sections.title: Implementation Best Practices and Team Selection
sections.summary: Select engineers with the best systems knowledge—the go-to people others seek when stuck. Go slowly with a phased approach. Experiment in non-critical systems first. Be honest: not everyone thrives. Curious, self-directed engineers who figure out how things are built will excel; those needing prescriptive specs will struggle. Deterministic verifiable tasks include feature flags, interactive elements, and analytics.

sections.title: Agentic Code Review and the Factory Metaphor
sections.summary: Code review split: agents handle style, naming, and opinionated conventions (removing emotional friction); engineers handle system design and big-picture decisions. Human involvement remains heavy on spec and LDD. Product/brand feel requires deliberate human attention. Spitz frames the engineering lifecycle as a factory of composable elements—branch naming, feature flags, API patterns—abstracted into reusable skills. Cautions against consuming third-party skills with contrasting software opinions.

sections.title: Automated QA, Self-Healing Agents, and Strategic Scaling Advice
sections.summary: After each PR merge, code auto-deploys to staging and a QA agent checks acceptance criteria against all related tickets, flagging failures. Near-term roadmap: agents automatically create fix PRs for failed criteria, enabling parallel self-healing and trust in autonomous flow. Humans remain essential for security, product/brand feel, and engineering complexity oversight—prescriptive LDDs prevent agent over-engineering. Strategic advice: start with boring repetitive tasks engineers hate for maximum buy-in, remove redundant process, encode engineering culture and patterns (e.g., service repository pattern) in skills, ensure guardrails are functional before autonomous flow, start with the best engineers, avoid onboarding everyone at once, and use a slow phased approach. Small companies have a scaling advantage; being too conservative risks compounding competitive gaps—months behind now can become a year behind quickly. Spitz invites the audience to scan a QR code to try the features.
